newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-TAKEOVER TALK SWIRLS AROUND MANCHESTER UNITED.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-TAKEOVER TALK SWIRLS AROUND MANCHESTER UNITED.

text.p: English soccer champions Manchester United were at the centre of feverish takeover talk on Friday after the club's chief executive said the team's financial success made it likely prey for big business.
"Any successful company is an attractive takeover prospect. People are going to look at it, so it could well be the subject of more takeover proposals," chief executive Martin Edwards told The Times.
Britain's Press Association quoted Edwards as saying that any proposals would be given serious consideration.
"...If it arises, then we would have to look at it as and when. We would have a responsibility to talk. But it would have to be in the best interests of the shareholders and the supporters."
The speculation sent United shares soaring to record highs of over five pounds ($7.9) on the London Stock Exchange -- valuing the club in excess of 300 million pounds.
The club, floated on the stock market five years ago, responded to the swirl of speculation with a statement that its board was not aware of any approaches from possible bidders.
Share prices dipped a touch after the statement but remained at just under five pounds, a gain of some 10 percent on the day.

United, Britain's best supported club, have filled the trophy cabinet and the bank coffers in recent seasons, delighting fans while winning the confidence of the growing army of city investors keen to put money into the game.
The club this week announced profits of over 15 million pounds following a season in which they won the coveted English league and F.A. Cup double.
Share prices have climbed from under two pounds at the end of January thanks to the playing success.
The rise has also been fuelled by a lucrative new television deal signed by the premier league with satellite broadcaster BSkyB which should treble television income for top English soccer clubs.

United are reported earlier this year to have rejected a takeover bid from publishing group VCI which valued the club at 300 million pounds. VCI did a deal with United in January to buy the publishing rights to club videos and books.
The Times article named brewer Whitbread and media and leisure group Granada as potential bidders.
It reported that Edwards, who has a stake of around 17 percent in United, has said privately that it would require a bid of over 400 million pounds to buy the club.
Sources close to Granada effectively ruled out a bid while Whitbread poured scorn on the suggestion.

"We would love to buy the club but there are as many beer drinkers in Liverpool, Newcastle and Chelsea," a spokeswoman said, adding that Whitbread would not want to do anything to upset customers who were fans of other clubs.
"The report is complete rubbish."
Share analysts say that the huge interest in soccer and the potential growth in revenue from pay-per-view television deals make a bid for United likely at some stage in the near future.

"Attendances are increasing, as is revenue from merchandising and BSkyB. If you were to add any revenue from pay-per-view, it would put nice icing on a nice cake," said Nicholas Knight of investment house Nomura.

Pay-per-view is expected to be introduced before the end of the century following the planned launch of digital satellite television by BSkyB late next year. It could generate tens of millions of pounds for clubs like United. ($1=.6350 Pound)
